name: LeFort 1 maxillary advancement

lead: A Le Fort I osteotomy is a horizontal cut through the upper jaw, made from inside the mouth, that lets the surgeon move the maxilla forward, back, up or down and fix it with plates. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a way to project the midface, support the area under the eyes and correct underbites, often paired with a lower-jaw operation.

The cut passes above the tooth roots and below the cheekbone and eye socket, freeing the tooth-bearing maxilla to be repositioned in three dimensions. Clinically it is used for bite problems, a recessed or vertically long upper jaw, cleft-related underdevelopment and, with lower-jaw surgery, sleep apnoea. Published studies document stability and outcomes in functional and cleft patients; there is little research on cosmetic-only advancement.

paras: Plates and screws hold the new position while bone heals, and orthodontics aligns the teeth around the operation. Surgery is done by oral and maxillofacial or craniofacial surgeons under general anaesthesia, with a months-long recovery. Forum members describe advancements of several millimetres and combination with lower-jaw surgery.

Documented concerns include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, relapse of the new position (greater for some movement directions and large advancements), nasal and lip changes and a months-long recovery. It is regulated as routine surgery.

angle.text: LeFort 1 moves the upper jaw forward to add midface projection, with the bone movement visible and measurable. The operation is standard for bite problems; claims of under-eye support rest mostly on bite and cleft research.

lead: Le Fort I osteotomy is an upper-jaw operation in which the maxilla is cut horizontally above the roots of the teeth, mobilised and fixed in a new position, usually through an incision inside the mouth.[1] It is the most common maxillary procedure in orthognathic surgery and can advance, set back, shorten, lengthen or widen the upper jaw.[2] For appearance, it is the operation that moves the midface itself: advancing the maxilla brings the cheek and upper-lip region forward, impaction shortens a long lower face, and rotation changes the angle of the bite plane. In looksmaxxing circles it is known as LeFort 1 or maxilla advancement.[3]

The procedure takes its name from the French surgeon René Le Fort, whose early-twentieth-century cadaver experiments classified facial fractures, the lowest of which is a horizontal fracture of the upper jaw above the palate.[4] Austrian surgeon Hugo Obwegeser developed the modern surgical version and is credited with first combining it with a lower-jaw operation.[5]

Clinical research on the operation comes mainly from bite-correction, cleft lip and palate and sleep apnoea patients. Reviews and studies report that its stability depends on the direction of movement, the fixation method and the technique, and that cleft patients often need maxillary advancement because earlier repair surgery can restrict maxillary growth.[6][7] Studies of purely cosmetic advancement are limited.

Forum discussions on looksmax.org describe advancement distances of several millimetres, counter-clockwise rotation, effects on lip seal and under-eye support, and combination with lower-jaw surgery; these are reported experiences rather than trial findings.[3][8][9]
infobox: René Le Fort, French surgeon who classified midface fractures[4]
Horizontal, above tooth-root tips and below the infraorbital foramen, through the maxillary sinuses (as described on forums)[8]
Advancement, setback, impaction, downgraft, rotation, expansion
Maxillary deficiency or excess, bite problems, cleft-related hypoplasia, sleep apnoea

paras: In Le Fort I surgery the upper jaw is separated from the rest of the midface along a horizontal line, which allows the tooth-bearing segment to be moved in three dimensions and then fixed with plates and screws.[1] It is used for deficiencies in the front-to-back dimension, for vertical excess of the maxilla (long-face pattern), and for transverse problems, sometimes with the maxilla split into segments.[1]

A review dedicated to the technique covers its indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, surgical technique and complications, and stresses close collaboration between surgeon and orthodontist and a sound grasp of facial analysis. Most reviews treat Le Fort I as one component of a larger plan that may include a mandibular osteotomy, a chin procedure and orthodontics.

Planning typically involves radiographs, photographs and three-dimensional software that predicts post-surgical appearance, and Wikipedia notes that presurgical braces can take up to a year, with surgery-first and clear-aligner approaches emerging.[1] A review of surgical management of vertical maxillary excess describes computer-assisted planning and virtual simulation as part of determining the individual surgical plan.[10]

One of the first published jaw-correction cases was reported by Simon P. Hullihen in 1849, and orthognathic surgery developed through the twentieth century, with maxillary and mandibular osteotomies in use from the 1940s.[1] The Le Fort name comes from René Le Fort, who studied facial trauma by dropping cadavers and described the horizontal, pyramidal and transverse fracture patterns, the first of which is the Le Fort I pattern.[4]

According to Wikipedia, Hugo Obwegeser trained under Richard Trauner at Graz and worked with Harold Gillies in 1951 and 1952, was influenced by Paul Tessier's methods for advancing the midface, and developed the modern Le Fort I procedure, which fully mobilises the maxilla by separating it from the pterygoid plates. Later animal research by William Bell confirmed that the mobilised maxilla retains its blood supply. Obwegeser introduced his orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons in 1966 and is credited with the first description of simultaneous upper- and lower-jaw surgery, combining a Le Fort I with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, dated to 1969 or 1970.[5]
From the 1970s rigid plate fixation reduced the need for long periods of jaw immobilisation, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[2]

Advancement of the maxilla is the movement most associated with midface projection. Because the cut is above the teeth, moving the maxilla forward moves the tooth-bearing upper jaw and the soft tissues attached to it, which surgeons use to improve profile balance in people with a recessed midface.[1][2] Impaction shortens the vertical height of the midface and reduces gum or tooth show in people with vertical maxillary excess, while rotation of the maxillomandibular complex changes chin and jaw position.[10]

A study of soft-tissue response after orthognathic surgery found that the midfacial soft-tissue response after maxillary advancement was minor, while procedures involving the mandible produced a stronger soft-tissue response, and facial surfaces generally became more symmetric and harmonious overall. A general encyclopedia summary likewise reports that advancing the maxilla by a few millimetres changes lip position by a smaller amount.[2]

The main medical indications are bite problems such as underbite and open bite, maxillary hypoplasia in cleft lip and palate, vertical maxillary excess, and airway problems. A review of anterior open bite discusses combined orthodontic and surgical approaches in which Le Fort I can be part of long-term correction.[11] Le Fort I with bone grafting is also used in some preprosthetic surgery before dental implants.[12]

Maxillomandibular advancement, which pairs a Le Fort I with a lower-jaw operation, is a treatment for obstructive sleep apnoea. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 22 patient populations (627 adults) reported that mean apnoea-hypopnoea index fell from about 64 to about 9.5 events per hour, with pooled surgical success of 86 percent and a cure rate of 43 percent; greater maxillary advancement was among the predictors of success, and major complications occurred in about 1 percent of patients.[13]

A frequently cited review of orthognathic stability reported that the predictability of surgical movements varies mainly with the direction of movement, then fixation type and surgical technique; superior repositioning of the maxilla was described as the most stable movement.[6]

A 2013 study of skeletal Class III patients defined relapse as a change greater than 2 mm or 2 degrees and found it in 24 percent of patients after two-jaw surgery and 21 percent after lower-jaw setback alone; the abstract reports that maxillary advancement was less prone to relapse than mandibular movement.

A randomised trial of splintless Le Fort I surgery compared patient-specific and conventional plates and found comparable one-year stability, with median translations under 1 mm and median rotations under 1 degree in both groups.[14] General encyclopedia summaries report that surgery usually produces a stable bite, improved chewing and high patient satisfaction; those figures come from an AI-generated overview and vary across the original studies.[2]

Diminished maxillary growth is a recognised consequence of cleft repair. A retrospective cohort study of 217 patients found that 37 of 177 non-syndromic patients (20.9 percent) needed Le Fort I advancement, including 47.4 percent of those with cleft lip and palate and none of those with cleft lip or cleft palate alone.[7] Reviews of cleft orthognathic surgery describe maxillary advancement, often with mandibular setback and other procedures, as altering profile and chewing and setting the stage for later lip and nasal revision.

In cleft patients with large deficiencies, advancement of more than 10 mm may be required, and distraction osteogenesis has been proposed as an alternative to conventional osteotomy for very large movements.[15][16] A meta-analysis found distraction tended to be preferred for younger patients with more severe deformities, with infection around the retained devices replacing some ischaemic complications of conventional surgery.[16] In a randomised trial the conventionally operated maxilla relapsed backward and upward over five years, while the distracted maxilla stayed forward, and the authors concluded distraction gave better long-term stability. A further randomised trial examined rigid fixation after distraction.

Human studies of Le Fort I surgery include a randomised trial comparing cleft maxillary distraction with orthognathic surgery over five years, a randomised trial of fixation after distraction, a randomised trial of patient-specific versus conventional fixation,[14] a clinical trial of soft-tissue response and facial symmetry using three-dimensional photogrammetry after orthognathic surgery, and a trial examining relapse after orthodontic therapy combined with surgery in skeletal Class III patients.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea pooled 627 adult patients from 22 populations to estimate efficacy and safety.[13] A meta-analysis of piezoelectric versus conventional saw techniques in orthognathic surgery compared blood loss, operating time and neurosensory disturbance across studies.[17] A clinical trial of 35 patients undergoing Le Fort I, sagittal split or two-jaw surgery tested taste at one, three and six months and found some changes in taste thresholds and intensity scores after Le Fort I.[18]

Registered trials include comparisons of two designs of patient-specific plates for Le Fort I fixation and of nasolabial changes with different alar base sutures after Le Fort I.[19][20] No published trial has been identified that tests Le Fort I advancement solely for cosmetic midface projection.

General descriptions of orthognathic surgery list bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and nerve-related numbness as the main immediate risks, with infection reported in up to 7 percent of cases in one source and some movements such as maxillary impaction carrying higher risk.[1] A 2024 review is dedicated to prevention and management of complications from Le Fort I osteotomy.[21]

Long-term concerns reported in cleft and Class III patients include skeletal relapse, which is a focus of the cleft distraction and relapse studies above.[15] Because the nasal base is attached to the maxilla, nasolabial changes after Le Fort I, including with different alar base sutures, are the subject of a registered trial.[20]

Wikipedia describes initial healing as taking two to six weeks and complete bone healing a further two to four months; jaw immobilisation may last one to four weeks, a liquid diet, swelling and weight loss are common, pain medication is typically needed for 6 to 8 days and return to work is possible at two to six weeks.[1]

Wikipedia lists jaw surgery among the 'hardmaxxing' procedures alongside rhinoplasty and says maxillofacial surgery is frequently proposed and discussed among looksmaxxers.[22] On looksmax.org, Le Fort I is discussed as a way to move the upper jaw forward and fix underbites, often alongside a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy and genioplasty, with members debating how much advancement looks natural.[3][8][9]

One user compiled a guide stating that advancement is typically in the range of 4 to 10 mm and describing options such as widening and rotation.[8] Another member reported 8 mm advancement and 5 mm impaction with a lower-jaw operation covered by insurance because of a severe underbite, and noted that 8 mm did not look as large as expected.[9] Other threads discuss the higher-level Le Fort II and III osteotomies, with one member asking whether a Le Fort II for a recessed maxilla alone is worthwhile and being told by another that this was not the procedure he would get.[23]

lore.intro: Forum threads treat Le Fort I as a core hard-tissue procedure for midface projection and underbite correction, usually part of a multi-surgery plan.[3][8][9]

claims.claim: Advancing the upper jaw also improves under-eye support and the infraorbital area.
Maxilla advancement of roughly 4 to 10 mm is the usual goal.
Le Fort I with a lower-jaw operation can be covered by insurance for an underbite.
Surgical movements are stable once healed.
Moving the upper jaw forward fixes a recessed midface without other procedures.
Higher-level Le Fort II and III osteotomies are an option for a recessed maxilla.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known jaw-correction cases.[1]
René Le Fort describes the facial fracture patterns that give the Le Fort I osteotomy its name.[4]
Maxillary and mandibular osteotomies come into use for bite problems and prognathism.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser works with Harold Gillies, later developing the modern Le Fort I procedure.[5]
Obwegeser introduces his orthognathic techniques to North American surgeons at a meeting in Washington, DC.[5]
Obwegeser is credited with the first description of combined upper- and lower-jaw surgery (1969 or 1970 depending on the account).[5]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces long jaw immobilisation, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[2]
A hierarchy-of-stability review ranks maxillary superior repositioning as the most stable orthognathic movement.[6]
Retrospective cohort study reports how often cleft patients need Le Fort I advancement.[7]
A systematic review and meta-analysis assesses maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnoea; a randomised trial compares five-year stability of cleft distraction and orthognathic surgery.[13]
Randomised trial of patient-specific versus conventional fixation reports comparable one-year stability.[14]
Review on prevention and management of complications from Le Fort I osteotomy published.[21]
